arguments.text: `parseDigits` returns `NaN` when the string has no parseable digits. It first tries `parseInt(str, 10)`; if that is NaN it walks the string converting Han decimal characters and any of the supported non-Latin digit ranges (arab, deva, thai, ...) into Latin digits, then returns `parseInt(value, 10)` — and since `value` is `""` when nothing matched, that final `parseInt("")` yields `NaN`. So `parseDigits("abc")`, `parseDigits("")`, `parseDigits("P1Y")` all give `NaN`, while e.g. `parseDigits("12")` gives `12`.

Full test suite: no regressions.

Fixed and verified. In `src/impl/util.js`, `objToLocalTS` reverted the 19XX legacy-year interpretation with `d.setUTCFullYear(d.getUTCFullYear() - 1900)`, which normalized day/month overflow against year 2000 (a leap year) instead of year 100 (not a leap year). It now uses `d.setUTCFullYear(obj.year, obj.month - 1, obj.day)`, so the overflow is normalized against the real year. E.g. `DateTime.fromISO("0099-12-31").plus({ days: 61 })` is now `0100-03-02` (was `0100-03-01`); the existing 100-barrier tests still pass. Full suite: no regressions.

Fixed and verified. `DateTime#isInDST` compared against `this.set({ month: 1 })`, which keeps the day-of-month; for years with year-round DST (1974 USA) January 6th onward is itself DST, so the comparison collapsed and isInDST flipped to false for every day >= 6. It now compares against `this.set({ month: 1, day: 1 })` (standard time). Verified for America/New_York 1974: false Jan 1-5, true Jan 6 through Oct 26, false Oct 27 (DST ended 2am that day) onward. Existing LA pre/during/post-DST tests still pass; full suite: no regressions.

Added `quarters: 4` to `years` in both matrices and `seconds: 91 * 24 * 60 * 60` to casual `quarters`.
